newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crudes see Dec grade business ebb wildly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crudes see Dec grade business ebb wildly.

text.p: Outright U.S. crudes ended weaker Monday, while December grades fluctuated wildly on the last day of trading before the pipeline scheduling cutoff.

Dec West Texas Sour/Midland dropped to trade at $4.55 below the Dec West Texas Intermediate/Cushing spot value. Traders said the sours came off on a "play" by a major trading company looking to depress WTS prices in order to benefit from pricing requirements for Ecuadorean Oriente.
Other wide numbers were traded for the Dec/Jan WTI roll, which was sold at $2.20, and Dec Postings at Cushing at $4.05.
Dec WTI ended at $25.75 a barrel, against Jan at $23.50-60.

Crude markets of all stripes were focused on Iraq Monday. Baghdad told the United Nations it accepted the oil-for-food deal terms unconditionally, dropping demands for influencing the way oil sales would be conducted and monitored.
Further, the United States said it would now approve the December pricing formula when the sanctions committee votes on the matter in the next week or so.
Prices retreated, but for many traders, the talk of a deal to bring the limited oil sales to market rang hollow.
"When it happens, you'll see excitement," said a cash trader, noting the unpredictable nature of both Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and the U.N. bureaucracy.
For the cash grades, the last deals for Dec business saw Midland/WTI done at 5 cts over the WTI, while Jan Midland was in similar trading ranges at flat to 6 cts above the marker.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James was traded at a 96 cts premium to the WTI/Cushing for Jan, and talked lightly at 80-90 cts over for the now expired Dec month.
Traders said other grades were quiet and uneventful, setting the pattern for the holiday week in the U.S..
"Anybody who needed to get things done in the last minute got them today. It will be even quieter on Tuesday," said a cash dealer.
Thanksgiving is celebrated on Thursday in the U.S..
